title: Effects of forest spatial types, element compositions and forest stands on restorative potential and aesthetic preference
research_question: 1. Which forest spatial types, element compositions and forest stands are more restorative and attractive? 2. What is the correlation between the restorative potential of forest spatial landscapes and aesthetic preference and fixation indicators?

participants.description: College students, ages 18-28 (mean age: 20.86±1.96 years), gender proportion 1:1, normal or corrected visual acuity, no illness, no smoking/drinking/coffee/functional drinks before experiment. From Sichuan Agricultural University, Chengdu City, China.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 42 photographs depicting typical forest landscapes, categorized by: 1) Forest spatial types (forest interior space (FIS), forest edge space (FES)); 2) Element compositions (pure forest (FO), 'forest +1 element' (F1: forest + roads, forest + architecture, forest + water), 'forest +2 elements' (F2: forest + roads + water, forest + roads + architecture, forest + architecture + water)); 3) Forest stands (coniferous (Co), broadleaf (Br), bamboo (Ba)). All photos taken with XT-100 camera, 16:9 ratio, good light (9:00-11:30, 14:00-16:30), no flash, no external interference, eye-level perspective. Photos were screened, added, deleted, and combined by professionals.

measures.instrument: Short-version Revised Restoration and Preference Scale (SRRPS) - average score of emotional, physiological, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions
Short-version Revised Restoration and Preference Scale (SRRPS) - score of one visual preference question
Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker system
Tobii Pro Glasses 2 head-mounted eye tracker system

findings.antecedent: Forest spatial type (forest edge space (FES) vs forest interior space (FIS))
findings.mechanism: Lower forest density, brighter forest edge environment, more open and transparent vision.
findings.quote: the restoration score of forest edge spaces (FES, 4.56) was significantly higher than those of the forest interior space (FIS, 4.19; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest interior space (F1: 'forest +1 element' and F2: 'forest +2 elements' vs FO: pure forest)
findings.mechanism: Adding landscape elements increases restoration.
findings.quote: the restoration scores of FIS1 and FIS2 (4.28 and 4.24, respectively) were significantly higher than those of FISO (3.78; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest edge space (F2: 'forest +2 elements' vs FESO: pure forest and FES1: 'forest +1 element')
findings.mechanism: Adding landscape elements increases restoration.
findings.quote: the restoration score of FES2 (4.95) was significantly higher than those of FESO and FES1 (4.49 and 4.20, respectively; p <0.01)

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest edge space (FESO: pure forest vs FES1: 'forest +1 element')
findings.mechanism: Pure forest foreground as a lawn, promoting relaxation.
findings.quote: the restoration score of FES0 (4.49) was significantly higher than that of FES1 (4.20; p <0.05).

findings.antecedent: Forest stand type (bamboo (Ba) vs coniferous (Co) and broadleaf (Br))
findings.mechanism: Cultural attributes (solid roots, straight stems, gentleman comparison), slender and straight trunks, light green leaf color.
findings.quote: the restoration score of bamboo forests (Ba, 4.53) was significantly higher than those of coniferous forests (Co, 4.33) and broadleaf forests (Br, 4.27; p <0.05).

findings.antecedent: Forest stand type in forest interior space (FIS-Ba vs FIS-Co and FIS-Br)
findings.mechanism: Cultural attributes, slender and straight trunks, light green leaf color.
findings.quote: the restoration score of bamboo internal space (FIS-Ba) was significantly higher than those of coniferous forests (FIS-Co) and broadleaf forests (FIS-Br)

findings.antecedent: Forest stand type in forest edge space
findings.mechanism: Open field of vision in forest edge spaces, subjects pay more attention to the outline of the forest, little difference in trunks and colors of the three forests.
findings.quote: the restoration score of forest edge spaces was not affected by different types of forests.

findings.antecedent: Forest spatial type (forest edge space (FES) vs forest interior space (FIS))
findings.mechanism: More open and transparent vision, broader view.
findings.quote: the aesthetic preference score of the forest edge space (FES, 5.04) was significantly higher than that of the forest interior space (FIS, 4.59; p <0.01)

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest interior space (F2: 'forest +2 elements' and F1: 'forest +1 element' vs FO: pure forest)
findings.mechanism: Richness of elements.
findings.quote: the aesthetic preference scores of FIS2 and FIS1 (4.64 and 4.63, respectively) were significantly higher than those of FISO (4.28; p <0.01)

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest edge space
findings.quote: the aesthetic preference scores of the forest edge spaces were not affected by different element compositions.

findings.antecedent: Forest stand type in forest interior space (FIS-Ba and FIS-Co vs FIS-Br)
findings.mechanism: Slender and straight trunks, neater appearance, light green/dark green leaf color.
findings.quote: significantly higher aesthetic preference scores for FIS-Ba and FIS-Co (4.80 and 4.62, respectively) than those of the FIS-Br (4.33; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Forest stand type in forest edge space (FES-Br vs FES-Co)
findings.quote: the aesthetic preference score (5.17) was significantly higher than that for the FES-Co (4.89; p <0.05).

findings.antecedent: Forest spatial type (forest interior space (FIS) vs forest edge space (FES))
findings.mechanism: More time interpreting the environment in FIS.
findings.quote: the total fixation duration of forest interior spaces (FIS, 6.34 s) was significantly longer than that of the forest edge spaces (FES, 5.74s; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest interior space (FIS2: 'forest +2 elements' vs FIS1: 'forest +1 element' and FISO: pure forest)
findings.mechanism: More elements require more interpretation.
findings.quote: the total fixation duration of FIS2 (6.59 s) was significantly longer than that of FIS1 (6.17s; p <0.05) and FISO (5.89s; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest edge space (FES1: 'forest +1 element' and FES2: 'forest +2 elements' vs FESO: pure forest)
findings.mechanism: More elements require more interpretation.
findings.quote: The total fixation duration of FES1 and FES2 (6.18 s and 5.90 s, respectively) for the forest edge spaces was significantly longer than that of FESO (4.20s; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest edge space (FES1 vs FES2)
findings.mechanism: Participants may not naturally pay more attention to images with multiple elements than to simpler photographs.
findings.quote: although no significant differences were observed, FES1 received more fixation duration than FES2.

findings.antecedent: Forest stand type (coniferous (Co) vs broadleaf (Br))
findings.mechanism: Coniferous forests depict straight trunks, leading to more concentrated and longer fixations.
findings.quote: the total fixation duration of coniferous forests (Co, 6.06s) was significantly higher than that of broadleaf forests (Br, 5.61 s; p <0.05)

findings.antecedent: Forest spatial type (forest interior space (FIS) vs forest edge space (FES))
findings.mechanism: More elements and complexity in FIS require more fixations.
findings.quote: the fixation count in forest interior spaces (FIS, 31.7-fold) was significantly higher than that in forest marginal spaces (FES, 30-fold; p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Element composition in forest interior space (FIS2: 'forest +2 elements' vs FISO: pure forest)
findings.mechanism: Higher fixation count in poor restorative environments (FISO) indicates more cognitive effort.
findings.quote: the fixation count of FIS2 (33.0-fold) was significantly higher than that of FISO (39.5-fold; p <0.01) for the forest interior spaces.

findings.antecedent: Perceived restorativeness (overall forest spatial landscapes)
findings.mechanism: Aesthetic preference plays a vital role in relaxation and decompression.
findings.quote: the restorative potential of forest spatial landscapes positively correlated with aesthetic preference (Table 2A; p <0.01)

findings.antecedent: Perceived restorativeness (overall forest spatial landscapes)
findings.mechanism: Less cognitive effort required in restorative environments.
findings.quote: negatively correlated with the total fixation duration and fixation count (p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Perceived restorativeness (overall forest spatial landscapes)
findings.mechanism: Less cognitive effort required in restorative environments.
findings.quote: negatively correlated with the total fixation duration and fixation count (p <0.01).

findings.antecedent: Perceived restorativeness (forest interior and exterior spaces with different stand types or number of elements)
findings.mechanism: Factors affecting forest environmental restoration merit further study.
findings.quote: additional correlation analysis indicated that the restorative potential was not related to aesthetic preference and fixation indicators (Tables 2B–D) in the forest interior and exterior spaces with different stand types or number of elements.

findings.antecedent: Aesthetic preference (forest interior space of broadleaf forests (FIS-Br))
findings.mechanism: Positive correlation between landscape spatial quality and fixation duration.
moderators_reported: forest interior space of broadleaf forests
findings.quote: a significant positive correlation between aesthetic preference and total fixation duration and fixation count was only observed in the interior space of broadleaf forests (FIS-Br; p <0.05; Table 3).

findings.antecedent: Aesthetic preference (forest interior space of broadleaf forests (FIS-Br))
findings.mechanism: Positive correlation between landscape spatial quality and fixation count.
moderators_reported: forest interior space of broadleaf forests
findings.quote: a significant positive correlation between aesthetic preference and total fixation duration and fixation count was only observed in the interior space of broadleaf forests (FIS-Br; p <0.05; Table 3).

findings.antecedent: Aesthetic preference (other forest spatial landscape characteristics besides FIS-Br)
findings.consequent: total fixation duration (TFD) and fixation count (FC)
findings.mechanism: Image fractal structure should be considered.
findings.quote: this study only found a positive correlation in the FIS-Br group. The perspective of image fractal structure should be considered in these types of studies.

mechanisms: Lower forest density and brighter forest edge environments provide higher recovery benefits.
Adding nature-mimicking landscape elements (architecture, water, roads) enhances restorative potential and visual response.
Well-maintained cultural and artistic elements are highly restorative and attract attention.
Pure forest foreground as a lawn in forest edge spaces promotes physical and mental relaxation.

Bamboo and coniferous forests (slender, straight, neat trunks; light green/dark green leaves) are perceived as more restorative and aesthetically pleasing than broadleaf forests (curved, chaotic trunks; yellow-green leaves).
More open field of vision in forest edge spaces reduces the impact of specific forest stand characteristics on restoration.
Higher visual complexity and element richness in forest interior spaces lead to longer total fixation duration and higher fixation count, indicating more interpretation effort.
Aesthetic preference is positively correlated with restorative potential, suggesting its role in relaxation and decompression.
Higher restorative potential is associated with shorter total fixation duration and lower fixation count, implying less cognitive effort in highly restorative environments.
Image fractal structure may influence the relationship between aesthetic preference and fixation indicators.
implementation_implications: Future forest landscape design should aim for lower forest density to create brighter and more open environments.
Integrate culture-related and art-related landscape components into forest design to enhance restorative potential and attractiveness.
Consider adding well-maintained paths or trails to increase readability and enhance restoration.
Prioritize bamboo and coniferous forests in interior forest spaces for higher restorative potential and aesthetic preference.
In forest edge spaces, pure forest (lawn-like) can be more restorative than adding single elements.

tables.description: Classification and meaning of forest spatial landscapes, detailing two forest spatial types, seven element compositions, and three forest stands.

Correlation results between the restorative potential of different forest spatial landscape characteristics and aesthetic preference and fixation indicators, broken down by spatial types, element compositions, and forest stands.
Correlation results between forest spatial aesthetic preferences and fixation indicators of different forest stand types.

limitations: The division of forest spatial landscape merits further optimization, as the study focused on simple compositions and basic landscape elements, omitting special elements like forest facilities and understory vegetation.

The architectures selected in the study had text, which might have confounded fixation data for buildings by attracting visual attention; future studies should use buildings without text and with simple colors.
The study only selected college students as subjects, limiting generalizability; future research should include participants of different ages and professional backgrounds.
Only 60 subjects were recruited, which could limit result accuracy; increasing sample size is advisable.
Photographs were taken in early autumn; differences in forest restoration and aesthetic preferences in other seasons should be considered.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: IntroductionAs global urbanization intensifies, the physical and mental stressors of modern life have led to the growing prevalence of suboptimal health conditions. Spending time in a forest benefits human health and well-being. In this context, based on the forest spatial types (forest interior and forest edge spaces), landscape elements (architecture, water and roads) and forest stands (coniferous, broadleaf and bamboo forests), this study investigated the effects of different forest spatial landscape characteristics on the restorative potential for college students, aesthetic preference and eye movement behavior (total fixation duration and fixation count).MethodsIn this study, a total of 60 subjects were exposed to 42 photographs depicting typical forest landscapes acquired through field studies. The Short-version Revised Restoration and Preference Scale and eye-tracking technology, were employed to study the recovery efficiency and visual attraction of forest spatial of different forest spatial types, element compositions and forest stands.Results(1) The restorative potential and aesthetic preference score of forest edge spaces were significantly higher than those of forest interior spaces. (2) The restorative potential of bamboo forests was significantly higher than those of coniferous and broadleaf forests. (3) In terms of forest interior space, the restorative potential of “forest + 1 element” composition and “forest + 2 elements” composition was significantly higher than that of pure forest, and the restorative potential of interior space of bamboo forest was significantly higher than those of coniferous and broadleaf forests. (4) In terms of forest edge space, the restorative potential of “forest + 2 elements” composition was significantly higher than that of pure forest, and the restorative potential of pure forests was significantly higher than that of the “forest + 1 element” composition. (5) The restorative potential of forest spatial landscape characteristics positively correlated with aesthetic preference and negatively correlated with total fixation duration and fixation count. These results can provide a reference for future forest landscape research, construction and management.
